description: Engineering team from DR Congo combining civil & electrical engineering, AI, data and programming. Our advantage: we connect physical understanding, scientific data and computational modeling to build practical solutions. Focused on microgravity combustion. Seeking physics, ML, software and aerospace skills.
summary:
Fire is a serious risk on crewed missions, and flames behave differently in microgravity. NASA has carried out many combustion investigations covering solid, liquid and gaseous fuels, flame spread, extinction, soot and smoke, yet their diversity makes it hard to find relevant experiments, judge whether they can be compared, and interpret them for a given question.
For the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 challenge “Flame in Freefall”, we built an interactive web prototype that makes these resources easier to use. We assembled an initial corpus of 24 investigations from the NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) and characterised it by fuel or material, phenomenon, experimental conditions, measured quantities and data types, with particular attention to when two investigations can legitimately be compared. The prototype combines a dashboard, to filter the corpus, with a chatbot, to query it in natural language using the information associated with the investigations, while keeping a path back to the investigations and sources used.
The limits are stated openly. In-depth comparison is not automated and remains subject to the user’s judgement, and chatbot answers depend on the coverage and quality of the corpus and on the underlying model. Artificial intelligence is used as an assistive layer over the data, not as a substitute for the original scientific data.
details:
Flame in Freefall is an interactive web platform designed to make NASA’s microgravity combustion research easier to explore, compare, and interpret in the context of spacecraft fire safety.

The project uses an initial corpus of 24 combustion investigations from NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI). These investigations cover solid, liquid, and gaseous fuels and phenomena such as ignition, flame growth and spread, extinction, burning rates, cool flames, soot formation, smoke generation, and large-scale fire behavior. We structured the investigations according to their fuels or materials, experimental conditions, measured quantities, phenomena, and available data resources.

The platform combines two complementary interfaces. An interactive dashboard allows users to search and filter investigations according to scientific and experimental criteria such as fuel, gravity, oxygen concentration, pressure, flow conditions, geometry, and measured phenomena. An AI-powered chatbot allows users to ask questions in natural language and obtain responses based on the information available in the investigation corpus. Users can then return to the underlying investigations and sources for verification.

The main benefit is to reduce the difficulty of navigating a heterogeneous scientific corpus. Instead of manually searching through numerous investigations and documents, researchers, engineers, and students can identify relevant experiments more efficiently and explore their characteristics through either structured filtering or natural-language interaction.

Scientific traceability is a central design principle. The system does not treat AI-generated responses as independent scientific evidence. The experimental context and original NASA sources remain essential for verification. We also considered the comparability of investigations: two experiments cannot necessarily be compared simply because they study the same phenomenon or share a variable. Factors such as fuel or material, gravity, oxygen concentration, pressure, flow conditions, geometry, experimental protocol, and measured quantity must be considered.

The intended impact is to make NASA’s microgravity combustion research more accessible and useful for understanding fire behavior in space. In the longer term, the platform could support researchers and fire-safety specialists in identifying relevant evidence and developing better-informed insights for human space exploration.

The prototype was developed as a web application using a structured scientific corpus, an interactive dashboard, and an AI chatbot. The project also uses structured data organization and scientific metadata to support search, filtering, and traceability. The current version focuses on demonstrating the concept rather than claiming fully autonomous scientific reasoning.

The project is creative because it combines scientific data exploration with natural-language interaction while keeping the user in the analytical loop. Rather than using AI simply as a chatbot, we use it as an interface to a specialized scientific corpus. This approach was designed around the actual characteristics and limitations of NASA’s combustion data.

Our team considered scientific comparability, data availability and quality, traceability, the risk of over-interpreting AI-generated information, and the limited development time of the challenge. For this reason, the current prototype does not claim to automatically perform reliable scientific comparisons across all investigations. It is designed primarily as an intelligent assistance tool for exploring and understanding NASA’s microgravity combustion research.
